findings.title: Gulf Crown's Saudi hotels fall inside the Al Noor GCC hospitality restriction
findings.quote: The Service Provider shall design, develop, test, deploy and support a revenue management and guest analytics platform for the Company's nine (9) Properties located in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as listed in Schedule 2.
findings.explanation: On the text, every element of Al Noor §12.1 is met: AtliQ Technologies Pvt Ltd is the same entity that signed with Al Noor; Gulf Crown owns and operates hotels (a 'Hospitality Business'); Saudi Arabia is named as a GCC state in Al Noor §1.9; the services are revenue-management and guest-analytics work; and §12.2 says it does not matter that the work is done from Pune. The restriction runs for the Al Noor Term (to 14 March 2028) plus 18 months, i.e. to 14 Sep 2029 if the Al Noor contract runs its full term, so the whole Gulf Crown delivery period (40 weeks, about to 17 Jul 2027 if signed on 10 Oct 2026) falls inside it. The only release is a written consent from Al Noor under §12.4, which is in Al Noor's sole discretion. The 10 Feb 2026 waiver does not help: it covers only demand-forecasting for Seaside Hotels LLC, Muscat, under the Seaside SOW, and expressly excludes any other Hospitality Business in Oman or elsewhere in the GCC and any Affiliate. This is a collision on the face of the text; what Al Noor could claim, and how its clause would be read, is for counsel.

register_refs.quote: the Supplier undertakes that neither it nor any of its Affiliates shall, during the Restricted Period, directly or indirectly, provide data analytics, artificial intelligence or revenue-management services to any Hospitality Business in the GCC.

For the purposes of Clause 12.1, services are provided "in the GCC" if the Hospitality Business receiving them is headquartered in, or the services relate to properties or operations located in, any state of the GCC, irrespective of where the services are performed.

"GCC" means the member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council, being the United Arab Emirates, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Qatar, the State of Kuwait, the Kingdom of Bahrain and the Sultanate of Oman.

"Hospitality Business" means any person, firm or entity that owns, operates, manages or franchises hotels, resorts or serviced apartments, or that provides distribution, revenue-management or guest-analytics services to any such person, firm or entity.
"Restricted Period" means the Term and the period of eighteen (18) months following the expiry or termination of this Agreement.

The Client may, in its sole discretion, waive the restriction in Clause 12.1 in respect of a specific engagement by written consent signed by an authorised signatory of the Client. Any such waiver shall be limited to its express terms.

This consent is strictly limited to the Seaside SOW. It does not extend to (a) any other services provided to Seaside, including any extension, renewal, change order or follow-on statement of work, unless separately consented to in writing by the Client; (b) any other Hospitality Business, whether in the Sultanate of Oman or elsewhere in the GCC; or (c) any Affiliate of the Supplier.

findings.title: Draft makes AtliQ warrant that no agreement restricts it from doing this work
findings.quote: it is not bound by any agreement or restriction which would prevent or restrict it from performing the Services for the Company.
findings.explanation: This is a warranty by AtliQ, not itself a restriction on AtliQ; the restriction comes from Al Noor §12. Given Al Noor §12.1 and §12.2, AtliQ could not give this statement as drafted without a carve-out or a written release from Al Noor. Signing it would add a second problem on top of F-01: a possible breach-of-warranty claim by Gulf Crown, against a draft that lets Gulf Crown deduct delay penalties from payments (§12.4). Whether the statement would be untrue in law is for counsel.

findings.title: Delay penalty is 1% of the whole contract per week, on any milestone, rounded up
findings.quote: Should the Service Provider fail to achieve any Milestone by its scheduled completion date, the Service Provider shall pay to the Company, by way of liquidated damages and not as a penalty, an amount equal to one percent (1%) of the Contract Value for each week or part thereof of delay.
findings.explanation: 1% x USD 140,000 = USD 1,400 for every week or part of a week of delay, capped at 10% x USD 140,000 = USD 14,000 in total (§12.3). The cap exists, so R-01 passes, but the rate is above Karandeep's recorded position (0.5% of the affected milestone fee per week, cap 5% of that milestone fee). Example: Milestone M1 is USD 21,000 (Schedule 3); a 1-week slip costs USD 1,400 here, about 6.7% of that milestone's fee. Gulf Crown may also deduct the amount from any payment (§12.4). The 10% total cap equals the figure Karandeep approved for Al Noor only, as a one-off.

findings.title: Only force majeure excuses delay; no excuse where Gulf Crown causes it
findings.quote: The Service Provider shall not be liable for delay to the extent such delay is caused by a Force Majeure Event as defined in Clause 15.
findings.explanation: Delay penalties run from 'Effective Date + N weeks' dates (Schedule 3). The only excuse is force majeure. Nothing excuses delay caused by Gulf Crown being late with system access, data or acceptance, and the draft has no acceptance period or deemed acceptance. The Brightwater dispute was exactly this gap: 19 days of client-caused delay, no exclusion in the contract, and a claim of USD 18,400.
